reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: DLE presents as well-defined, coin-shaped, erythematous plaques with adherent scale, follicular plugging, and a tendency to leave central scarring, atrophy, and dyspigmentation
Lesions favour sun-exposed areas such as the face, ears (including the conchal bowl), scalp, and neck, and are typically photosensitive
Scalp involvement can produce permanent scarring alopecia, so early recognition and treatment matter for hair preservation
Most patients have skin-limited disease, but a minority progress to or coexist with systemic lupus erythematosus, so ask about systemic symptoms and monitor over time
Strict photoprotection with sun avoidance, clothing, and broad-spectrum sunscreen is a cornerstone of management alongside topical and systemic anti-inflammatory therapy
Smoking worsens disease activity and reduces treatment response, so cessation advice is an important part of care
Long-standing DLE plaques, especially on the lip or in scars, carry a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma, so biopsy non-healing or changing lesions
Histology and immunofluorescence showing interface change and immune deposition at the dermo-epidermal junction support the diagnosis in uncertain cases
reference.pathophysiology: Discoid lupus erythematosus is a chronic autoimmune interface dermatitis in which ultraviolet light and other triggers provoke keratinocyte injury and expose nuclear antigens. A cytotoxic lymphocytic response targets the basal epidermis, producing vacuolar degeneration at the dermo-epidermal junction, follicular plugging, basement-membrane thickening, and a perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate. Immune complex and complement deposition at the junction can be demonstrated on direct immunofluorescence. Sustained inflammation destroys adnexal structures, leading to the scarring, atrophy, and permanent alopecia characteristic of established lesions. Genetic predisposition, ultraviolet exposure, and smoking all contribute.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus with cutaneous involvement
Lichen planus, including follicular (lichen planopilaris) on the scalp
Psoriasis or actinic keratoses on sun-exposed sites
Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising within a chronic plaque
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with routine histology and direct immunofluorescence
Autoantibody screen (antinuclear and related antibodies) and assessment for systemic lupus
Baseline bloods and urinalysis to screen for systemic involvement
Ophthalmological screening where antimalarial therapy is planned
Repeat biopsy of any non-healing, indurated, or ulcerated long-standing plaque to exclude malignancy
redFlags: Non-healing, ulcerated, or enlarging chronic plaque (particularly on the lip) suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Emergence of systemic symptoms (arthralgia, renal, haematological, or constitutional features) indicating progression to systemic lupus
Rapidly progressive scalp involvement threatening permanent scarring alopecia
Features suggesting overlap with other connective tissue disease
Significant disfigurement causing psychological distress that needs support
reference.prognosis: Skin-limited discoid lupus often follows a chronic relapsing course; with photoprotection and treatment many lesions become inactive, but scarring, dyspigmentation, and alopecia may be permanent, and a minority of patients evolve towards systemic lupus, warranting periodic review.
pitfalls: Failing to counsel on photoprotection and smoking cessation, both of which strongly influence outcome
Attributing scarring alopecia to other causes and delaying treatment until hair loss is irreversible
Not screening for systemic lupus or overlooking its later emergence
Missing malignant transformation within a chronic plaque
Underestimating the cosmetic and psychological burden of facial scarring
management: Strict photoprotection with sun avoidance, protective clothing and broad-spectrum sunscreen as a cornerstone of care
Topical or intralesional corticosteroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors for active plaques
Antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine as first-line systemic therapy for widespread or refractory disease
Second-line systemic immunomodulation for resistant disease with methotrexate, mycophenolate, dapsone or oral retinoids
Smoking cessation advice, as smoking worsens disease activity and reduces treatment response
Ophthalmological screening before and during antimalarial therapy
Periodic review with bloods and urinalysis to detect progression to systemic lupus erythematosus
Re-biopsy of any non-healing, indurated or ulcerated long-standing plaque to exclude squamous cell carcinoma
